analysis.one_liner: Caps Senate campaign spending, bans PAC money, cuts individual donation limits to $100, and gives candidates free TV time.
analysis.headline: Paul Wellstone's campaign finance overhaul was introduced in May 1993 with no cosponsors, sent to the Senate Rules Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let Senate candidates voluntarily accept strict spending limits in exchange for public benefits: government payments matched to small in-state donations, 90 minutes of free prime-time broadcast time, and discounted campaign mail. In exchange, candidates could spend at most $25,000 of their own money, face spending caps tied to state population, and a $100 cap would replace the $1,000 limit on individual donations. It would also have banned political action committees from federal elections, restricted party 'soft money,' limited lobbyists' role in campaign giving, and required candidates to say 'I approve this message' on the air.
analysis.who_benefits: Senate candidates without personal fortunes or ties to big donors, who would have gotten public funds matched to small contributions, free broadcast time, and cheap mail to level the field against wealthy self-funders and PAC-financed rivals. Voters would have gained shorter disclosure thresholds, immediate reporting of big independent spending, and prominent disclaimers on who paid for ads.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Candidates without rich donors or PACs

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who accept the limits get government payments matched to donations of $100 or less from in-state residents, plus free prime-time broadcast time and nonprofit-rate campaign mail.
Individual contribution limits would drop from $1,000 to $100, and multicandidate PACs would be barred from federal elections entirely.

Candidates could spend no more than $25,000 of their own or their family's money, and unlimited spending by a non-participating opponent would trigger matching payments and unlock extra limits for the eligible candidate.

Independent spending of $5,000 or more would have to be reported within 48 hours (or 24 hours in the final 20 days before an election), and ads would need large, readable 'who paid for this' disclaimers with the candidate appearing on camera to approve them.

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees and the industries that fund them would lose their channel of direct influence; broadcasters would have to donate 90 minutes of prime airtime per candidate; national and state party committees would lose most of their unregulated 'soft money' fundraising; large individual donors and wealthy self-financing candidates would see their influence capped.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, big donors, broadcasters, party committees

drawbacks.text: The spending limits collided with the Supreme Court's Buckley v. Valeo line of cases; the bill itself concedes the risk by requiring expedited Supreme Court review and voiding the entire act if its core limits are struck down.

The Senate Election Campaign Fund relies on voluntarily designated contributions and penalty payments, with only a non-binding 'sense of the Senate' on future funding, leaving the public financing on uncertain fiscal footing.

A $100 contribution ceiling could push campaign money toward independent groups and party committees; the bill tries to counter this by counting coordinated spending against a candidate's cap, but enforcement would rest heavily on FEC audits.
Requiring broadcasters to provide free prime time imposes a real cost on local stations, and the 90-minute mandate applies only to candidates who opt into the system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have cut special-interest money out of Senate campaigns substantially, but its own text shows the authors knew the spending caps were legally fragile, and its public funding mechanism was left half-built. It was an ambitious, somewhat unwieldy attempt at reform rather than a carefully engineered one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules Committee on the day it was introduced and never came out; no hearing, no vote, nothing until Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Wellstone introduced the bill on May 13, 1993, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
No member joined as a cosponsor.
The only action after referral was a repetition of Wellstone's introductory remarks more than a year later, on October 5, 1994; the committee never reported the bill.
The bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent senators and the organized interests, large donors, and party committees that fund them are better off, since the existing campaign finance rules carried over unchanged. Broadcasters also avoided the mandated free airtime.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in May 1993 and reiterated his introductory remarks in October 1994; no other senator joined him.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never reported it, held no recorded action, and let it expire without a vote.

against.name: Wendell Ford
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the two years it sat pending.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew zero cosponsors, so no party split is visible in the record; it was sponsored by a Democrat and died in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would ban multicandidate PACs from making contributions or expenditures in federal elections entirely, eliminating the channel through which organized business and interest groups fund Senate campaigns.
Stations would have to give each qualifying Senate candidate 90 minutes of free prime-time airtime in the 60 days before an election, plus meet stricter ad disclaimer rules.

National and state party committees would lose the ability to raise unregulated 'soft money' for federal elections, though they would gain a new $5,000-per-person allowance for grassroots voter registration and turnout work.

industries.industry: Wealthy self-funding candidates and large individual donors
industries.note: Personal spending would be capped at $25,000 and individual contributions cut from $1,000 to $100, removing the advantage of candidates with personal fortunes and donors able to give large checks.
The bill restricts contributions routed through intermediaries and conduits and bars certain lobbyist contributions, tightening rules that currently let hired representatives bundle access.
